title: Antelope Wells House
summary: Walls up. A house that faces the mountains and turns a thick, windowless back to the west wind.
story:
The clients bought 10 acres with a well and a view of Antelope Wells. Their brief was one sentence: 'We want to hear the wind, not feel it inside.'

We tested their soil in phase 01 — it rammed well with 8% cement. The plan is a single bar: living in the middle, beds at the ends, every room with a door to a shaded court on the east. The west wall is earth, 18 inches, no glass.

Regret so far is below — I put it in writing while we can still fix the next one.
materials: Rammed earth (site soil), standing-seam roof, concrete floors
regret: I specced the roof color from a screen. On site it read blue. We repainted the sample, not the roof — and I now approve every exterior color standing in the desert at noon.

title: Chinati View Cabin
summary: In drawings. A weekend cabin that can be left alone for months and opened in an hour.
story:
A Houston couple wanted a place that didn't need babysitting. Thick walls hold temperature through empty weeks; shutters close the glass court; the cistern and solar are sized for four-day stays.

The drawing set is the product right now — if they never build, they own a complete, priced set of drawings.
materials: Rammed earth, steel shutters, cistern, solar
regret: None yet — drawing stage. The risk I am watching is the access road cost, which may eat the porch.

title: My Own House on San Antonio St
summary: The first one. I live in the experiment, including its mistakes.
story:
I drew my own house to learn what I was asking clients to live with. 18-inch walls, no west window, a kitchen that is also the office.

Seven summers in: indoor temperature swings 6 degrees on a 30-degree day. The mistake is the bathroom — see regret.
materials: Rammed earth, adobe interior plaster, mesquite
regret: The bath is too far from the bedrooms and I walk through the cold court at night. In every plan since, beds and bath share a wall.

title: Goat Pen Studio
summary: A painter's studio that doubles as guest quarters, built on an old goat-pen slab.
story:
We kept the slab and the fence line. North glass for painting, earth walls on the other three sides, a murphy bed and an outdoor shower.

Smallest project I have built, and the most used — she paints daily and guests fight over it.
materials: Rammed earth, north glass, outdoor shower
regret: I made the studio door 30 inches to save wall. Her canvases are 36. We cut the opening wider in year two — measure the work, not the person.

title: Valentine Schoolhouse Rework
summary: A 1938 schoolhouse kept standing: new roof, earth-plaster inside, classrooms become a house.
story:
The building was sound and the town wanted it kept. We insulated inside with earth plaster so the brick face the town knows stayed untouched.

Classrooms map surprisingly well to a house: two become bedrooms, one becomes a kitchen that seats fourteen.
materials: Existing brick, earth plaster, new steel roof
regret: I underestimated the roof. Old trusses needed sistering throughout — contingency is now 15% on any reuse, written into phase 01.

title: Llano Wind House (unbuilt)
summary: Complete drawings, never built. Listed anyway — paper houses are part of a practice.
story:
The clients' well came in at half the expected flow and they paused, then moved for work. The drawings are complete and permitted in this story.

I keep unbuilt work in the index because it shows how I draw, and because pretending only built work exists is marketing, not a record.
regret: I designed to the view before the well test came back. Now water is phase 01, before any design — that order is in the process page because of this house.
